planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop, since this slender heirloom bolts quickly once temperatures climb.

directions: This traditional variety from Provence produces slender, tapered roots about three to four inches long, colored two-thirds scarlet red fading to a crisp white tip. It matures notably fast and holds its mild, non-pithy flavor longer in the ground than rounder spring radishes, making it forgiving of a missed harvest day. Thin seedlings early to give roots room to elongate rather than swell, and keep the bed evenly moist to prevent cracking. Popular with market growers and home cooks alike for slicing into butter-and-radish openers in the French style.

common_name: Philadelphia White Box Radish (Historic American Window-Box Radish)

planting.note: Direct sow shallowly in loose, fertile soil as soon as it can be worked, succession sowing every two weeks; this compact heirloom also performs well in shallow containers and window boxes.

directions: Developed by Philadelphia seedsmen in the late nineteenth century from older European white radish stock, this heirloom forms small, round, pure-white roots with crisp, mild flesh. It was bred specifically for the shallow soil of urban window boxes and tight market-garden rows, so it tolerates closer spacing than most globe radishes without turning woody. Harvest promptly once roots size up, since white-skinned types show pithiness quickly in warm weather. A reliable choice for gardeners wanting an authentic nineteenth-century American market variety rather than a modern hybrid globe.

planting.note: Direct sow into very deeply worked, stone-free sandy loam at least a season's worth of weeks before the first fall frost, since the root can grow a meter or more and needs loose soil with no obstruction to elongate fully.

directions: Traditionally grown in the soft, sandy riverbank soils near Nagoya, this extraordinary daikon produces one of the longest edible roots of any vegetable, commonly exceeding a meter with only a slender two-inch diameter. Deep, stone-free, well-irrigated soil is essential, since the root follows the path of least resistance and will fork or stunt in compacted ground. It is grown chiefly for moriguchizuke, a specialty pickle made by repeatedly aging the root in sake lees over several years, so roots are typically pulled whole with care to avoid snapping the brittle tip. Given the long growing season required, gardeners outside its native river-valley climate should expect a correspondingly later harvest window.

common_name: Chonggak Radish (Altari Mu, Korean Ponytail Radish)

planting.note: Direct sow in fertile, loose soil in late summer for the classic fall kimchi harvest, thinning so finger-sized roots and their leafy tops both have room to develop.

directions: Named for its leafy top said to resemble the braided ponytail worn by unmarried young men in old Korea, this small white radish is harvested whole, leaves and all, while the root is still finger-sized and tender. Both the crisp root and its slightly peppery greens are used together, most famously fermented whole into chonggak kimchi, so plants are grown at closer spacing than daikon-type radishes and pulled young rather than left to bulk up. It prefers the same cool fall conditions as other Asian radishes and resists pithiness well if kept consistently watered. Because the greens are eaten along with the root, avoid any mulch or soil splash that would leave grit between the leaf ribs.
